                                                                    Detection with Diffusion

                                         1. Introduction                                                      techniques. Among these, reconstruction-based methods
                                                                                                              emerge as a natural solution which train models to learn
                                         Visual Anomaly Detection (AD) involves identifying and               normal sample reconstructions. During inference, when
                                         localizing abnormal regions in images, with applications             an anomalous sample is encountered, the model will at-
                                         across various computer vision tasks. These include qual-            tempt to reconstruct it as a normal sample, resulting in
                                         ity control in manufacturing [2, 46, 67] where detecting             a higher reconstruction error compared to normal inputs.
                                         defects ensures product reliability, and autonomous driv-            This reconstruction error is then used to identify anoma-
                                         ing [5] where identifying unseen obstacles is crucial for            lies. Various architectures have been explored for this
                                         safety. The key challenge in visual AD lies in the scarcity          purpose, including autoencoders [1], masked vision trans-
                                         of labeled abnormal samples—while normal cases are of-               formers (ViTs) [60], and Mamba models [19]. Recently,
                                         ten well-documented, collecting and annotating anomalous             diffusion-based [22, 39, 44] approaches have been pro-
                                         instances is typically impractical due to their rarity and di-       posed for AD [20, 30, 48, 49, 57, 62] as another line of
                                         versity [35]. Consequently, unsupervised approaches that             reconstruction-based methods. However, first, their perfor-

Figure 2. The processing pipeline of VLMDiff. During training (top), a normal (i.e. anomaly-free) image is fed to both 1) an off-the-
shelf VLM (on the right) to extract the detailed description of the object using the query (PD ), which is further encoded into condition
vector c using text encoder, and to 2) a pretrained image encoder (note that we finetune the image autoencoder using only normal images
beforehand) to get the latent vector. Then, a diffusion process adds noise to the latent vector and learns to denoise it with the guidance
coming from the condition vector. During inference (bottom), the same process as training is followed, except there is no text description
is used to condition the diffusion model. The denoised latent code is fed to the pretrained image decoder to get the reconstructed image.
Anomaly segmentation is done by finding the dissimilar locations on the feature maps of input and reconstructed normal images.

6.2. COCO-AD per split results
Per-split results on COCO-AD [59] are shown in Table 14.
VLMDiff shows a noticeable improvement compared to the
baselines, especially in the first split where there are signif-
icantly fewer normal images.
